Di Oro MaxBrew filters coffee very well - I bought this to replace an older reusable K-cup device bought years ago that didn't make very good coffee. The Di Oro MaxBrew does an excellent job of filtering coffee. I have almost no residue in my cup. It also holds considerably more coffee than my old one and so lets me brew good, strong coffee even when using the large cup setting on the Keurig at my office. I am very pleased with it. One tip I have is to make sure to use expresso ground coffee (I like Café Bustelo). Also, make sure to fill the cup just to the top of the screen opening. Don't bother dealing with LG or Service people! - After owning our LG front loading washer (WM2487HRMA) for only 5 years the drum stopped spinning, I did a little research to find the problem and it turns out this part failed and it is part of the motor, that little sticker on the front of the machine I've been looking at for the last 5 years says the motor has a 10 year warranty LG says you have to hire a LG certified service tech that comes with a $100.00 trip charge and you have to pay labor to replace, I was told it's an average cost of $100.00-$175.00 depending on your area, I found a video on youtube walking you through the whole process.

Tools required are a Phillips screw driver, a 17mm wrench or 17mm socket wrench, and lock-tight for assembly, you can get locktight at a hardware store or automotive parts store

Unplug power cord
Remove the 4 screws on the back panel
Remove the 17mm bolt on the rotor, you may need someone to hold the drum from spinning it will be a little hard to remove (lefty lucy, righty tighty)
slide the rotor off
Check stator for damage (if the motor ran the stator should be fine, also easy to replace)
Line up the splines on the shaft with the splines on the rotor and slide the new rotor on
reinstall bolt with locktight
reinstall panel
Done!

I read some reviews complaining that the ice doesn’t break automatically—I actually appreciate this very much because that also means it holds longer. You just take the ice sheets from the bottom of the stack, and then they’re easier to break, too. The machine also keeps it fairly cold, and it makes a boatload of ice in a day. Batches aren’t as “instant” as the bullet-style, but it doesn’t take that much longer, lasts much better in a drink, and if you just keep it filled and let it run, there’s always some ready. I’ve been doing this since I got it—I let it run all day and night. I leave it in the strainer without transferring to the freezer and use lots of ice throughout the day. If I ever have to buy another, I’ll buy this brand, but it’s been very reliable and consistent, so I’m not even sure I’ll have to get another. I suppose if you could shell out $400-500 for a luxury kind, you might be able to find a better one, but I’m exceedingly happy with this one, especially for the price. Research, Diagnose, change out all items that may fail.. - My 20 year old dryer decided that it was going to heat at it's hottest setting to the point of scalding my hands when removing the clothes from the dryer and causing a major case of wrinkles in my work Polo's. After going to YouTube to find out how to diagnose the issue, I found that there are a few things to check. First thing you will need to do is open the back of the dryer, with it unplugged, and check the Thermal Fuse. This can be done with a multi-meter or temporarily jump the two connectors/blade terminals and check if the Dryer runs at the correct temp for all cycles. Since I had the dryer taken apart I figured I would clean out the blower fan area and the fan ducting as well as the entire "innards" of the dryer. After temporarily jumping the thermal fuse I found that it had kicked the bucket as the dryer started to work again due to jumping out the fuse. Did I say that this dryer is 20 years old and the original fuse lasted that long? So I decided that since I have the thing open I might as well replace the other 20 Year old electrical components that were back there. These Items included: the Thermal Fuse, Cycling Thermostat, High Limit Dryer Thermostat and Dryer Thermal cut off. Each have their own job and purpose, so don't skimp out and think you can get away with changing the item that has failed, because if that item failed the others will follow. Did I mention my Dryer is 20 years old? As A side note; I also checked the Heating Element and found that one of the coils had warped and contacted/welded itself the the element body, this is what took out the fuse. A pair of needle nose pliers and a steady hand detached the coil and re-positioned the coil in its original shape and placement. My 20 year old dryer, that was a wedding gift to my wife when she married her fist husband now works like a champ!
